newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk Islamist sect members in anti-secular trial.
newsitem.headline: Turk Islamist sect members in anti-secular trial.

text.p: A Turkish court resumed the trial on Wednesday of more than 100 Islamist sect members charged with threatening Turkey's secular order.
Only one of the 127 defendants for the Aczmendi group was in the courtroom as lawyers began their defence in the Ankara state security court.

"This is a political trial," said Cuneyt Toraman, a lawyer for the defendants. He said demands by the powerful National Security Council for a crackdown on religious groups and activities would affect the verdict.
"The verdict is obvious anyway. The NSC has taken a decision," he told Reuters at the court before the trial began.

The Aczmendis, who grow long hair wrapped in turbans and carry long staffs in what they say is imitation of the Prophet Mohammad, were detained at a rowdy ceremony in Ankara last year at which they clashed with police.
The defendants are also accused of insulting the founder of modern Turkey, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, during "zikr", a ceremony at which sect members dance themselves into a frenzy.
The majority of the defendants were earlier remanded in custody pending a verdict. They could face three to 10 years in jail if found guilty.

Group members wear dark flowing robes in contravention of Turkey's strict laws against Islamic dress. The powerful army has demanded the Islamist-led government fully enforce a ban on Islamic dress as part of a crackdown on religious activism.
"This court can give them any punishment it wants because it does not like the way they dress and the appeals court will approve it," Toraman said.
The court imposed a nominal fine on the defendants last month for wearing their religious clothes at the trial and told them not to attend the hearings if they wore their conventional dress.
The one defendant present in court on Wednesday wore a long blue shirt and baggy trousers.
Ataturk outlawed Islamic sects in the 1920s but the groups have quietly flourished again in recent years.

Turkey's first Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan came to power last June at the head of a coalition with conservatives. However, the form of Islam he represents is far milder than that of the Aczmendis.
